theme: Gideon called; the fleece; the 300; victory and aftermath
readingInstruction: Read Judges 6:1-8:35. This is a long reading, so read it in three movements: Gideon’s call and the fleece (chapter 6), the victory with three hundred men (chapter 7), and the aftermath (chapter 8). Keep in mind the verse that stands behind the story: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.”
settingTheScene: Israel has again done evil, and this time the Midianites oppress them so severely that the people hide in caves and mountain strongholds. Every harvest is stripped by swarms of raiders “like locusts.” Into this misery God sends a prophet to remind Israel why they are suffering, and then he sends an angel to a farmer named Gideon, who is threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites. Gideon is not the obvious choice for a hero. The stories that follow show a man who is hesitant, who tests God, and who triumphs only because God shrinks his army to nothing. But they also show how quickly a victory can become a snare.
observation: The angel of the LORD greets Gideon, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor” (6:12), while Gideon is hiding.
Gideon objects, “My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (6:15).
He tears down his father’s altar of Baal and Asherah by night, and is nicknamed Jerubbaal (6:25-32).
Gideon asks for a sign with the fleece, first wet with dew while the ground is dry, then the reverse (6:36-40).
God reduces the army from 32,000 to 10,000 to 300, “lest Israel boast over me” (7:2-8).
The 300 carry trumpets, empty jars, and torches, and shout, “For the LORD and for Gideon!” (7:16-20).
The Ephraimites complain that they were not called sooner, and Gideon soothes them with a gentle answer (8:1-3).
Gideon refuses the kingship but makes an ephod from the gold, which “became a snare to Gideon and to his house” (8:22-27).
After the victory, the land has rest for forty years, but when Gideon dies Israel again goes after the Baals (8:28-35).
interpretation:
The angel’s greeting is deliberately ironic. “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” Gideon is at the winepress, hiding. God speaks to who he will make him, not who he is now. This is a pattern in the Bible: God sees what he will do through the person, not just their present weakness. Gideon’s response is one of honest objection. “If the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us?” It is a real question, and God does not scold him for it. Instead, God answers with a promise: “I will be with you.”

Before Gideon can defeat the Midianites, he must deal with idolatry at home. God tells him to tear down his father’s altar to Baal, and Gideon does it at night, afraid of the people. It is a small act of faith with big consequences. The first battle is always internal. We cannot expect God to defeat our enemies while we shelter our idols.

The fleece story is often misread as a model for guidance. In fact, Gideon had already received a clear word from God, and the fleece shows his unbelief. Still, God graciously answers. The lesson is not that we should seek signs, but that God is patient with weak faith. The better way is to trust his word without needing proof.

The reduction of the army is the center of the story. God says that 32,000 is too many “lest Israel boast over me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” Twenty-two thousand leave out of fear, and the remaining 10,000 are reduced to 300 by their way of drinking water. The strategy makes the victory unmistakable. Three hundred men with trumpets, jars, and torches defeat a host “like locusts in abundance.” The point is not the cleverness of the plan but its absurdity. God’s power is made perfect in weakness, as Paul will say in 2 Corinthians 12:9.

But the story does not end in triumph. In chapter 8, Gideon deals with Ephraim wisely, but takes brutal revenge on the towns that refused him supplies. He refuses the crown with the right words, “The LORD will rule over you,” but then asks for gold and makes an ephod. The ephod becomes an idol, and “all Israel whored after it there.” The man who tore down Baal’s altar ends by building a rival object of worship. Even the best of the judges fail. The people forget God as soon as Gideon dies. The tragedy shows that Israel’s problem is not just a lack of leaders but a hardness of heart. It is a heart problem that no judge can fix.
connection: The call of Gideon echoes Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3-4). The shrinking army anticipates 1 Samuel 14:6 and 2 Chronicles 20. The smashing of the jars to reveal the light is echoed in 2 Corinthians 4:7, “we have this treasure in jars of clay.” The ephod’s failure recalls the golden calf of Exodus 32. Gideon appears in Hebrews 11:32 as a man of faith. The principle of strength through weakness is expressed in 1 Corinthians 1:27-29.
application:
Think of how God sees you. Gideon was addressed as a “mighty man of valor” while he was hiding. In Christ, you are called a saint, a child of God, and a new creation. Ask the Lord to help you live into what he says you are.

Examine the “ephod” risk. After a spiritual success, we can be tempted to build a monument to ourselves or to something that distracts from God. What victories in your life might become a snare if you start to trust them?

Finally, embrace your weakness. If you feel inadequate for what God has put before you, hear the point of the 300. He chooses small instruments so that the glory is his.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to tear down the idols in your house.
Thank him that he wins with the weak, and tell him where you feel weak.
Ask him to keep you from boasting in yourself.
